opus-5.5.text:
I think it matters a lot, but maybe not in the way people first expect. If a lab's view is that catastrophic risk is very low, say well under one percent, then a responsible scaling policy looks like cheap insurance. You're committing to things you don't expect to bind for a while: "if we see these dangerous capabilities, we'll stop or put these protections in place." If you don't think you'll hit those thresholds soon, signing up costs little, and it's a nice way to show you're taking the concerns seriously.

If a lab thinks the risk is quite high, then the policy is much more consequential, because you actually expect the conditions to trigger. Then the question is whether you can meet the protective measures in time, or whether you'll be forced to pause. Some people in that position are enthusiastic, because this is exactly the mechanism they want. Others worry it gives false comfort, a framework that makes scaling seem safe when it isn't.

The part I find most important is that a good policy is supposed to be robust to disagreement about risk. You don't need everyone to agree on whether the probability of catastrophe is two percent or twenty percent. You need agreement on something more concrete: if a model can meaningfully help someone build a bioweapon, or can autonomously replicate and evade shutdown, then we shouldn't deploy it, or even train further, without security and safeguards adequate to that level of danger. People with very different overall views can often agree on that conditional. That's what makes it a useful coordination point, both between labs and as a basis for eventual regulation.

The flip side is that how seriously a lab takes the risk shows up in the details: how conservative the thresholds are, how much margin they leave for being wrong about capabilities, how good their evaluations are, and whether they'll actually follow through when it's commercially costly. Two labs can have policies that look similar on paper and behave very differently when the bar is actually hit. So I'd watch less whether a lab has a policy and more whether it's specific, externally checkable, and whether they've said in advance what they'll do if they can't meet the commitments.

r001.rationale: The candidate says labs that see high risk may find policies more consequential, but does not state that labs viewing catastrophic harms as plausible within roughly five years tend to be more interested in them.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it matters a lot, and in a fairly direct way. If you're a lab that thinks catastrophic risk is real but not imminent—that the models we have today are clearly not dangerous, but that models a few years out might be—then responsible scaling policies are kind of the natural thing to want. The whole point of an RSP is to say: we're not going to pause now, because there's no reason to pause now, but we're going to commit in advance to what evidence would make us stop, and to what safeguards we'd need before continuing. That framing is very appealing if you believe the risk is real but conditional on capabilities you don't have yet.

If a lab thinks the risk is essentially zero, or that it's the kind of thing that will obviously be fine once we get there, then an RSP looks like pure cost. You're binding your own hands, you're creating evaluations that might slow you down, and you're doing it for a scenario you don't believe in. You might still adopt one for reputational or regulatory reasons, but you won't invest in making it actually bite, and I think the quality of these policies depends a lot on whether the people writing them actually believe the thresholds could be crossed.

And then at the other end, if you think catastrophic risk is very high and very near, you probably don't think scaling is responsible at all, and an RSP looks like a fig leaf—a way of saying "we'll be careful" while continuing to do the dangerous thing. I have some sympathy for that view, but I'd say the RSP approach is partly a bet that it's better to have labs make concrete, falsifiable commitments than to have them make no commitments because the only commitment that would satisfy the most worried people is one they won't make.

So I'd say the sweet spot for RSPs is labs that are genuinely uncertain, take the tail risks seriously, and want some mechanism for turning that concern into action rather than just vibes. One of the things I find most valuable about them is that they force a lab to write down, in advance, what would change its mind. That's useful even if the lab's current estimate of the risk is fairly low, because it creates an external standard that people can hold them to later, when there's a lot more commercial pressure to rationalize continuing.

r001.rationale: The response says labs that see catastrophic risk as real and think models a few years out might be dangerous are naturally drawn to responsible scaling policies.

astra-6.text:
I think it matters a lot whether the lab thinks catastrophic risk is a real possibility. If you think there’s a substantial chance that more capable models could pose catastrophic risks, then you have a pretty strong reason to want some process for deciding when it’s safe to keep going. A responsible scaling policy is one way to make that concrete: what capabilities would concern us, how would we detect them, and what safeguards would we need before proceeding?

If you think those risks are basically implausible, then the motivation is more likely to be reassuring the public or heading off regulation. And you might still support a policy, particularly if you expect its thresholds never to be reached. So agreement on having a policy can conceal quite a lot of disagreement about the underlying risk.

The important question is what happens when following the policy becomes costly. If your evaluations suggest that you need to pause or invest substantially in safety, do you actually do that? That’s where the difference between treating this as a serious risk-management exercise and treating it as a communications exercise becomes consequential.

r001.rationale: The response says labs that see a substantial chance of catastrophic risk have stronger reason to want responsible scaling policies, but it does not specify that the harms are plausible within roughly five years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on why the lab thinks the risk is low. If your view is, “These systems aren’t going to be capable enough to pose a catastrophic risk anytime soon,” then a responsible scaling policy should be relatively easy to accept. You’re saying, “We’ll check whether they have those capabilities, and if they do, we’ll need stronger safeguards before proceeding.” On your own view, that shouldn’t be a binding constraint for a while.

If you think the risk is substantial, then you have a more direct reason to want that policy. You want some mechanism that prevents competitive pressure from pushing you into deploying systems you can’t adequately control.

The harder case is someone who thinks the systems will become very capable, but that the risks will be manageable, while also being skeptical that we can measure either the danger or the adequacy of the safeguards. They might worry that a policy will stop useful development for reasons that don’t track actual risk. And I think that’s a real disagreement you have to engage with: what evidence would justify continuing, and what evidence would justify stopping?

So I wouldn’t interpret willingness to adopt a responsible scaling policy as a straightforward measure of how worried a lab is. A lot depends on what the policy actually commits them to, and whether those commitments remain meaningful when following them becomes costly.

r001.rationale: The response says that labs viewing catastrophic risk as substantial have a direct reason to want a responsible scaling policy, but it does not specify that the risk is plausible within roughly five years.
